_about: Single source of truth for every rendering, and the auditable term ledger (check 5). ONE rendering per referent for the whole book. Before you romanize any name, check here. status per entry: 'attested' (form used in English scholarship, give the citation in note), 'provisional' (your romanization, not found in outside sources), 'decided' (a project style call). If you find a better attested form mid-book, change it here AND grep every built chapter for the old form, then rebuild. Sections are rendered as glossary headings; keys starting with '_' are ignored. Add/rename sections freely (people, organizations, places, terms, ...).

陈恭澍.cast: The author and narrator. A Juntong operative who ran the Beiping and Tianjin stations in the 1930s, commanded the Shanghai District, directed the 1939 Hanoi attempt on Wang Jingwei, and led a special unit in the 1946–49 civil war.

戴笠.cast: Courtesy name Yunong (雨农). Founder and lifelong head of the Juntong, the Nationalist secret service, and Chen's chief; died in a 1946 air crash.

汪精卫.cast: Founding Nationalist leader who broke with Chongqing in 1938 to seek peace with Japan and headed a Japanese-sponsored government at Nanjing; target of the 1939 Hanoi attempt.

张敬尧.note: 1881–1933; Beiyang general and former military governor of Hunan, assassinated in Beiping in 1933.

孙传芳.note: 1885–1935; Beiyang warlord, later assassinated by Shi Jianqiao.

施剑翘.note: Avenger who shot Sun Chuanfang dead in 1935; publicly pardoned.

吉鸿昌.note: 1895–1934; Northwest Army general, figure in the 1933 Chahar anti-Japanese army; executed by the Nationalists. Honoured as a Communist martyr in the People's Republic.

冯玉祥.note: 1882–1948; the 'Christian General,' a powerful and often-shifting warlord.

石友三.note: 1891–1940; a general notorious for switching sides repeatedly.

殷汝耕.note: 1885–1947; head of the Japanese-sponsored East Hebei regime; executed as a traitor after the war.

王克敏.note: 1879–1945; head of the Japanese puppet 'Provisional Government' at Beiping; called 'Blind Wang.'

刘绍勷.note: The 'Southwest delegate' killed by mistake in the 1934 Tianjin attempt on Ji Hongchang; romanization uncertain.

陈璧君.note: 1891–1959; Wang Jingwei's wife, a forceful political figure; imprisoned after the war.

曾仲鸣.note: 1896–1939; Wang Jingwei's close aide, killed at Hanoi in the attack meant for Wang.

李士群.note: 1905–1943; ex-Communist who ran the Wang regime's secret police at No. 76; poisoned by the Japanese.

傅筱庵.note: 1872–1940; banker installed as puppet mayor of Shanghai; assassinated in 1940.

张啸林.note: One of the Green Gang's 'Three Tycoons' of Shanghai; killed in 1940 for collaborating.

郑介民.cast: Dai Li's deputy in the secret service; the Juntong's special commissioner for North China and Chen's direct superior at Beiping. Rose to full general.
郑介民.note: Senior Nationalist intelligence chief; rose to full general.

毛人凤.note: Dai Li's successor as head of the postwar secret service (the Baomiju).

毛泽东.note: Leader of the Chinese Communist Party; Chen calls him 'the bandit chief Mao' throughout.

林彪.note: Communist commander whose army took Beiping and Tianjin in 1948–49.

聂荣臻.note: Communist commander in the North China campaign of 1948–49.

刘少奇.note: 1898–1969; PRC head of state, purged and hounded to death in the Cultural Revolution.

陶铸.note: Senior Communist official, another victim of the Cultural Revolution.

唐英杰.note: Member of the Hanoi action team; romanization mine.

余鉴声.note: Member of the Hanoi action team; romanization mine.

王鲁翘.note: Member of the Hanoi action team; romanization mine.
王鲁翘.cast: A Shandong man and former bodyguard of Dai Li; co-lead of the Hanoi action team.

郑修元.note: Secretary of the Shanghai District headquarters; romanization mine.

张亚民.note: Wireless operative sent to Shanghai; romanization mine.

毛万里.note: Juntong officer stationed at Yanshan, Jiangxi; romanization mine.

山本荣治.note: Japanese adviser who shielded Wang Kemin in the 1938 attempt; the Japanese reading is reconstructed from the Chinese characters.

大冢清.note: Former Japanese military-police officer at Nanjing; the Japanese reading is reconstructed.

中岛信一.note: Japanese Ume Kikan captain who shielded Chen; the Japanese reading is reconstructed.

冈村.note: Japanese Kempeitai Tokkō section chief at Shanghai; the Japanese reading is reconstructed.

王天木.cast: Chief of the Tianjin Station and an old friend of Dai Li's; born Wang Renqiang, he worked under the cover name Zheng Shisong. A central figure in the Hanoi affair to come.
王天木.note: A senior Juntong operative in North China; later, in the Hanoi affair and after, his loyalties became a matter of dispute.

范行.cast: Courtesy name Jiman. A mysterious intelligence source recruited by the Beiping Station, whose true identity and allegiance Chen chased for twenty-one years.
范行.note: Courtesy name Jiman; romanization mine. The 'great international spy' of this section, a thread that runs to 1949 and beyond.

白世维.note: Seventh-class academy graduate; the gunman who carried out the 1933 killing of Zhang Jingyao, the Beiping Station's first case.

杨英.note: One of the three-man team, with Chen and Qi Nanpu, that founded the Beiping Station; romanization mine.

戚南谱.note: Member of the founding Beiping Station team; later killed by the Communists in his native Anhui. Romanization mine.

吴泰勋.note: Courtesy name Youquan, called 'the Fifth Master'; son of the Manchurian general Wu Junsheng, and a wealthy patron of Dai Li's work. Chen honours him as a 'nameless hero.'

李士珍.note: Whampoa graduate and police theorist, the strict team leader of the Honggongci training class; later a leading figure in the Nationalist police and a rival of Dai Li for its control.

黄雍.note: Courtesy name Jianqiu; a first-class Whampoa graduate who took Chen in at Nanjing and recommended him into the work.

张炎元.note: Courtesy name Binghua; a second-class Whampoa graduate and early Juntong figure who shared lodgings with Chen at Nanjing.

张作霖.note: 1875-1928; the 'Old Marshal,' warlord of Manchuria, killed by the Japanese Kwantung Army in the Huanggutun bombing of 1928.

胡汉民.note: 1879-1936; a leading Kuomintang theorist and rival of Chiang Kai-shek. Feeds back to authority.json on completion.

张学良.note: 1901-2001; the 'Young Marshal,' son of Zhang Zuolin; his 1936 seizure of Chiang at Xi'an forced the anti-Japanese united front. Feeds back to authority.json on completion.

何应钦.note: 1890-1987; senior Nationalist general, at this time acting head of the Military Affairs Commission's Beiping Branch.

坂垣征四郎.note: 1885-1948; general of the Japanese Kwantung Army, an architect of the 1931 Manchurian seizure; hanged as a war criminal. The source writes 坂垣 for the standard 板垣.

赵庭贵.note: Zhang Jingyao's chief of staff, lodged with him at the Grand Hôtel des Wagons-Lits; romanization mine.

应元勋.note: Proprietor of the Yingyuantai tailor shop, called 'Manager Ying'; his unwitting remark exposed Zhang Jingyao's room. Romanization mine.

飞龙.note: Working name ('Flying Dragon') of the courtesan of the Flower-Cultivating House who served as Wang Tianmu's cover at the hotel.

含春.note: Working name of a courtesan of the Flower-Cultivating House in Hanjiatan, an acquaintance of Wang Tianmu's.

张宗昌.note: 1881-1932; warlord of Shandong, the 'Dog-Meat General.' See the note in this section.

蔡锷.note: 1882-1916; Yunnan general who launched the 1915 National Protection War against Yuan Shikai's monarchy. See the note in this section.

小凤仙.note: The sing-song girl of Republican legend who helped Cai E flee Yuan Shikai's Beijing in 1915; a stock figure of stage and screen.

宋哲元.note: 1885-1940; commander of the Twenty-Ninth Army in North China. See the note in this section.

段祺瑞.note: 1865-1936; Beiyang premier and head of the Anhui clique. See the note in this section.

施从滨.note: Division commander under Sun Chuanfang, executed by him at Bengbu; the killing his daughter Shi Jianqiao avenged in 1935.

吉章简.note: Nationalist gendarmerie officer, commander of the Fourth Regiment and leader of Chen's Lixingshe cell; later a general. The source's stray '古章简' is the same man.

蒋孝先.note: Commander of the gendarmerie's Third Regiment and a kinsman of Chiang Kai-shek's; killed in the 1936 Xi'an Incident. Romanization mine.

韩文焕.note: Gendarmerie battalion commander in Chen's Lixingshe cell; romanization mine.

丁昌.note: Gendarmerie Third-Regiment adjutant in Chen's Lixingshe cell; romanization mine.

宣侠父.note: Communist organizer who, with Ji Hongchang, formed the 1934 Chinese People's Anti-Fascist Grand Alliance at Tianjin.

南汉宸.note: Communist figure, co-organizer of the 1934 Tianjin alliance; later the founding governor of the People's Bank of China.

王子襄.note: A qualified Western-trained physician made chief of the Tianjin Station on Chen's recommendation to Dai Li; he died in 1934 while testing a poison, and Chen reckons him a fallen comrade of the service.

王玉梅.note: Wang Zixiang's younger sister, a noted Beiping society beauty; through her Dai Li entered Beiping's polite society.

吕一民.note: Chief of the Tianjin Station's Intelligence Group, seconded to Chen for the Ji Hongchang case.

吴萍.note: A Tianjin Station veteran; the look-out and cover man in the Ji Hongchang operation.

王文.note: Cover name of Wang Wenhan (王文翰), a Beiping Station action man; the gunman whose shots killed Liu Shaorang by mistake.

郑恩普.note: A former Henan military officer at leisure in Tianjin, drawn into Chen's Military Group; addressed as 'Third Master Zheng.' He later married Yang Yushan.

杨玉珊.note: A liaison of the Tianjin Intelligence Group; her nerve fixed Ji Hongchang's room at the Guomin Hotel.

陈国瑞.note: Yang Yushan's younger brother, a strapping youth pressed into service as a runner in the operation.

任应岐.note: A former Zhili-clique general drawn into Ji Hongchang's circle; extradited and executed alongside Ji in 1934, though, as Chen notes, not himself a Communist.

穆欣.note: The Communist author of the 1979 booklet 'General Ji Hongchang,' which Chen quotes at length and disputes.

吴佩孚.note: One of the foremost warlords of the 1920s and head of the Zhili clique.

佟麟阁.note: Later a Nationalist general and a celebrated martyr of the 1937 defense of Beiping.

杨虎城.note: The Shaanxi general who, with Zhang Xueliang, seized Chiang Kai-shek in the 1936 Xi'an Incident.

李大钊.note: A co-founder of the Chinese Communist Party, executed at Beiping in 1927.

王芃生.note: Head of the Nationalist Institute for International Affairs, a noted intelligence analyst on Japan.

先鸿霞.note: Wang Wen's boyhood friend and fellow townsman, an attendant adjutant to Shi Yousan; drawn in for the Shi Yousan operation of late 1934, in which he was taken by the Japanese gendarmerie and lost.

曾澈.note: Secretary and later District chief of the Juntong's Tianjin organization, and head of the Anti-Japanese Traitor-Killing Corps; martyred at Beiping in 1940.

方炳西.cast: A member of the Hanoi team who arrived first and rented the safe house; a fluent French speaker and one of the operation's few survivors.

齐庆斌.note: Chief of staff of the Luan-Yu Guerrilla Command.

陈资一.note: Head of the Tianjin Station after Chen's departure; martyred.

周世光.note: Head of the Beiping Station; martyred.

胡永荃.note: A volunteer worker of the Tianjin Station who escorted Chen to Shanghai.

陈春圃.note: A kinsman of Chen Bijun and an official in the Wang Jingwei regime.

晴气庆胤.note: Colonel and deputy chief of the Ume Kikan, successor to Kagesa Sadaaki; the Japanese reading is reconstructed.

影佐祯昭.note: Japanese army officer who headed the Ume Kikan and engineered Wang Jingwei's defection.

刘原深.note: A contributor whom Chen engaged to analyze Wang Jingwei's character from his poetry.

近卫文麿.note: Prime Minister of Japan; issued the three statements of 1938 that Wang Jingwei answered.

林柏生.note: An associate of Wang Jingwei who arranged the publication of the Yan Telegram at Hong Kong.

高宗武.note: A Nationalist diplomat who conducted the secret 1938 Shanghai talks with Japan on Wang's behalf; later broke with him.

梅思平.note: A negotiator of the secret 1938 Shanghai agreement for Wang Jingwei.

今井武夫.note: Japanese army officer, a principal in the secret talks with Wang's representatives.

伊藤芳男.note: A South Manchuria Railway adviser who helped mediate the 1938 Shanghai talks; Japanese reading reconstructed.

吴敬恒.note: Better known by his courtesy name Zhihui (稚晖); a venerable Nationalist elder statesman who drafted the resolution expelling Wang.

张继.note: A veteran Nationalist and member of the Central Standing Committee.

陈布雷.note: Chiang Kai-shek's confidential secretary and chief speechwriter.

剑秋.note: One of two senior colleagues (an 'elder brother') with whom Chen dined and Dai Li in Nanjing in 1932; full identity uncertain.

炳华.note: The given name of Zhang Yanyuan (张炎元), an early Juntong figure; see that entry.

汪兆铭.note: The original name of Wang Jingwei (汪精卫); see that entry.

岑家焯.note: A senior Whampoa (third class) schoolfellow of Chen, Guangdong man; sent to Hanoi to assist the operation.

余乐醒.note: Hunan man, France-trained doctor of chemistry; deputy director of the Linli Training Class, sent to Hanoi as the unit's chief of staff and technical adviser.

龙云.note: The Yi military strongman who governed Yunnan 1927–45; his Kunming was a way-station on Wang Jingwei's flight.

有田.note: Arita Hachirō (有田八郎, 1884–1965), Japan's foreign minister 1936–40.

田中义一.note: Japanese premier and foreign minister 1927–29; associated with the Jinan Incident and the alleged Tanaka Memorial.

金雄白.note: Journalist of the Wang Jingwei regime; wrote its history under the pen name Zhu Zijia.

朱子家.note: Pen name of Jin Xiongbai (金雄白); see that entry.

用五.note: Pen name of the anonymous author of the diary of Wang's flight quoted here, published in the Hong Kong magazine Zhanggu; true identity unknown.

张季鸾.note: Chief editorial writer of the Dagongbao (Ta Kung Pao), a celebrated political commentator.

甘乃光.note: Nationalist official; the diarist 'Yongwu' consults him on Wang's flight.

陈树人.note: Nationalist elder and painter, cited on the causes of Wang's flight.

彦慈.note: A nephew of Wang Jingwei, left behind in Chongqing after Wang's flight.

孙哲生.note: Sun Ke / Sun Fo (孙科, 1891–1973), son of Sun Yat-sen; 'Zhesheng' is his courtesy name.

彭学沛.note: Vice-minister of Communications in the Nationalist government.

陈公博.note: A close associate of Wang Jingwei who followed him into the collaborationist regime; later its head, executed 1946.

周佛海.note: A leading figure in Wang Jingwei's peace movement and later regime.

广田.note: Hirota Kōki (广田弘毅, 1878–1948), Japanese foreign minister and later premier; author of the 1935 'Three Principles.'

重光葵.note: Japanese diplomat, ambassador to the USSR at the time of the Zhanggufeng Incident.

袁世凯.note: President of the Republic of China 1912–16; recipient of Japan's Twenty-One Demands in 1915.

何芝园.note: Now a National Assembly delegate; in 1938 chief of the Second Section (intelligence) of the Bureau of Investigation and Statistics.

徐先生.note: A pseudonym. The 'special personage' at Hanoi who aided the operation from behind the scenes; his real name Chen withholds.

曾先生.note: A Fujianese go-between supplied by Mr. Xu; distinct from Zeng Che and Zeng Zhongming. Chen forgot his given name.

魏春风.note: A quick-witted young overseas-Chinese guide at Hanoi, raised in Annam; the team's local navigator.

阮小姐.note: Wei Chunfeng's Annamese sweetheart; gave cover and reconnaissance help. Surname Nguyễn.

曹师昂.note: Hunan-born aviator, French military-aviation graduate; flew for the French Volunteer Air Squadron. Sent to Hanoi by Dai Li.

谭天堑.note: A melancholy Hunan man, French-trained in finance, just released from Xifeng detention; on a separate secret mission at Hanoi.

张逢义.note: Shandong man, Military Academy seventh class; a Beiping Station Action Group member in Book One, sent to Hanoi.

陈步云.note: A taciturn man of Xuzhou in Jiangsu, sent to the Hanoi action team.

黄强.note: Courtesy name Mujing; director of the Haiphong office of the Southwest Transport Administration.

稽小姐.note: A courier who brought three Browning pistols from Hong Kong to Haiphong; herself one of the service's people.

罗君强.note: Named in the 'Yongwu' diary; a figure in Wang Jingwei's Chongqing circle.

陈皋.note: Named in the 'Yongwu' diary as one who handled affairs at the Wang residence.

谷正鼎.note: A Nationalist official sent to Hanoi to see Wang; his report is quoted via the 'Yongwu' diary.

王宠惠.note: Styled Liangchou; jurist and Foreign Minister of the National Government.

宋子文.note: T. V. Soong; financier and statesman, charged to urge Wang to go to Europe.

魏道明.note: Styled Bocong; a Nationalist official who asked Chen after Wang's movements.

王芄生.note: Head of the 'Institute of International Affairs,' which specialized in international intelligence.

大屋久寿雄.note: Hanoi correspondent of Japan's Dōmei news agency, possibly doubling as an intelligence agent (reading provisional).

汪兆镛.note: Wang Jingwei's elder half-brother, a Guangxu provincial graduate and painter-chronicler of Lingnan; his stern tutor.

汪兆辛.note: A cousin of Wang Jingwei who recommended him as a household tutor.

朱执信.note: Revolutionary and husband of Wang Jingwei's eldest sister; a fellow Tongmenghui founder.

梁启超.note: Styled Rengong; reformist thinker and leader of the Emperor-Protection (Royalist) party, rival to the revolutionaries.

黄兴.note: Styled Kexing; co-founder with Sun Yat-sen of the Tongmenghui and chief military leader of the 1911 revolution.

章太炎.note: Given name Binglin; eminent classical scholar and revolutionary, editor-in-chief of the Min Bao, driven off by Wang.

宋教仁.note: Tongmenghui leader and architect of parliamentary Nationalism, assassinated in 1913 on Yuan Shikai's order.

陶成章.note: Revolutionary who, with Zhang Taiyan, set up the rival Restoration Society (Guangfuhui).

吴樾.note: Revolutionary whose 1905 attempt to bomb the five ministers sent to study constitutions inspired Wang's own plot.

黄复生.note: Originally Shuzhong; Wang Jingwei's co-conspirator in the 1910 attempt on the Prince Regent, imprisoned with him.

罗世勋.note: A participant in the 1910 plot against the Prince Regent.

载沣.note: Prince Chun, the Prince Regent for the child Xuantong emperor; target of Wang's 1910 assassination attempt.

善耆.note: Prince Su, the Qing Minister of the Interior who examined Wang and spared his life out of regard for his talent.

廷杰.note: Qing Minister of Punishments who urged Wang's beheading.

袁克定.note: Eldest son of Yuan Shikai, who drew Wang into secret talks with his father.

杨度.note: Politician who went south with Wang in the 1912 peace talks; later a promoter of Yuan Shikai's monarchy.

鲍罗廷.note: Mikhail Borodin, the chief Soviet (Comintern) adviser to the Nationalist Party in the 1920s.

马林.note: Henk Sneevliet ('Maring'), early Comintern representative to China.

越飞.note: Adolph Joffe, Soviet diplomat whose 1923 declaration with Sun Yat-sen framed the KMT-Soviet alliance.

陈炯明.note: Guangdong warlord who rebelled against Sun Yat-sen in 1922.

陈独秀.note: Co-founder and first General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party.

周恩来.note: Chinese Communist leader; later premier of the People's Republic.

叶挺.note: Communist commander in the 1927 Nanchang and Guangzhou uprisings.

贺龙.note: Communist commander in the 1927 Nanchang uprising.

张发奎.note: Nationalist general who circulated a telegram mocking Wang's two-facedness.

沈崧.note: Styled Cigao; Wang Jingwei's nephew and agent, killed at Hong Kong.

顾孟余.note: A leading figure of Wang's faction who declined to follow him to Nanjing.

郑学稼.note: Writer whose 1939 essay on Wang Jingwei (in The Spirit of the Age) Chen quotes.

吉冈文六.note: Japanese writer who likened Wang to a boneless flesh-worm (reading provisional).

唐有壬.note: A soft, 'feminine' associate of Wang's clique, named as already dead; assassinated in 1935.

陈畊基.note: A rich Panyu émigré at Penang, head of the 'Little Orchid Pavilion' club; father of Chen Bijun.

刘子蕃.note: Colleague of Wang Zhaoyong whose sister was betrothed to Wang Jingwei, then jilted.

袁尹白.note: Wang Jingwei's sister's husband, under whom the young Wang practiced calligraphy.

孙中山.note: Founder of the Chinese Republic and the Tongmenghui; called the Father of the Nation (国父) and the Party Leader (总理).

董其昌.note: Ming-dynasty painter-calligrapher of tender grace, whose hand Wang's writing most resembled.

元遗山.note: Jin-dynasty poet Yuan Haowen (styled Yishan), a couplet of whose ci Wang echoed in his last poem.

陈邦国.note: Anhui man, seemingly risen from the ranks; the big, powerful 'open-road vanguard' of the Hanoi raid, one of the three captured (seven years). The source spells his surname 陈 (Chen) in Chapter 5 and in the quoted Biography of Dai Yunong, but 郑 (Zheng) in Chapter 3; rendered throughout as Chen Bangguo. Romanization mine.

方君璧.note: 1898-1986; painter, wife of Zeng Zhongming; wounded in the Hanoi attack.

朱媺.note: Second daughter of Zhu Zhixin; lodged in the Wang house at Hanoi and survived the attack.

何文杰.note: Wang Jingwei's son-in-law, husband of Wang Wenxing; present at the Hanoi attack.

汪文惺.note: Wang Jingwei's eldest daughter, wife of He Wenjie.

陈国琦.note: A nephew of Chen Bijun (Wang's wife's side); wounded in the leg in the Hanoi attack.

戴芸生.note: An attendant in the Wang household at Hanoi; wounded in the arm.

何就.note: The cook in the Wang household at Hanoi; wounded in leg and arm.

陈国星.note: An attendant in the Wang household at Hanoi; slightly wounded in the chest.

汪圯.note: Wang Jingwei's secretary; raised the alarm from a window after the Hanoi attack.

于右任.note: 1879–1964; revolutionary elder, calligrapher, and president of the Control Yuan; a standing member of the Supreme National Defense Council named in the quoted meeting record.

居正.note: 1876–1951; veteran Tongmenghui revolutionary and jurist, president of the Judicial Yuan.

孔祥熙.note: 1881–1967; H. H. Kung, financier and Chiang's brother-in-law; acting president of the Executive Yuan and finance minister, who received Trautmann's overture.

翁文灏.note: 1889–1971; geologist and technocrat, a senior figure in the wartime government.

邵力子.note: 1882–1967; journalist and Nationalist official, later a peace envoy to the Communists.

陈立夫.note: 1900–2001; with his brother Chen Guofu the head of the 'CC Clique' and the party's organization apparatus.

陈果夫.note: 1892–1951; elder of the 'CC Clique,' brother of Chen Lifu.

董显光.note: 1887–1971; Hollington Tong, US-trained journalist and the government's chief spokesman for foreign publicity.

张群.note: 1889–1990; close associate of Chiang, foreign minister 1935–37; secretary-general of the Supreme National Defense Council.

徐堪.note: 1888–1969; financial official, later minister of finance.

徐谟.note: 1893–1956; vice-minister of Foreign Affairs who accompanied Trautmann and reported the mediation to the meeting; later a judge of the International Court of Justice.

顾祝同.note: 1893–1987; senior Nationalist general (courtesy name Mo-san / 墨三).

白崇禧.note: 1893–1966; the Guangxi general (courtesy name Jiansheng / 健生), one of Chiang's foremost strategists.

唐生智.note: 1889–1970; general (courtesy name Meng-xiao / 孟潇) who had commanded the defense of Nanjing.

徐永昌.note: 1887–1959; general (courtesy name Ci-chen / 次宸); director of the Military Operations Board. The source's '次展 / 次辰' are misprints for 次宸.

陶德曼.note: Oskar Trautmann, German ambassador to China, whose winter-1937 mediation the quoted meeting record concerns (identified at ch13).

川樾.note: Kawagoe Shigeru, Japanese ambassador to China 1936–38, who negotiated with Foreign Minister Zhang Qun in 1936.

秦桧.note: d. 1155; the Song chancellor who engineered the judicial murder of the general Yue Fei and made peace with the Jin; the archetypal Chinese traitor, whose kneeling iron effigy stands before Yue Fei's tomb at West Lake.

李完用.note: 1858–1926; the Korean prime minister who signed the 1910 treaty annexing Korea to Japan; a byword for a national traitor.

吴三桂.note: 1612–1678; the Ming general who opened the Shanhaiguan pass to the Manchus in 1644, letting the Qing conquest through.

溥仪.note: 1906–1967; the last Qing emperor, installed by Japan as the puppet ruler of 'Manchukuo' in 1932.

哈柴.note: Emil Hácha, president of rump Czecho-Slovakia, who in March 1939 signed his country to Germany and stayed on as puppet 'State President' of the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia.

张伯伦.note: Neville Chamberlain, British prime minister, whose Munich Agreement of September 1938 pressed Czechoslovakia to cede the Sudetenland to Germany.

苏锡文.note: A collaborator official under the Japanese in the lower Yangtze; cited here as a puppet turned on by his own guards.

李石曾.note: 1881–1973; anarchist and Nationalist elder, with Wu Jingheng a leader of the Franco-Chinese work-study movement.

张溥泉.note: Courtesy name of Zhang Ji (张继, 1882–1947), veteran Tongmenghui revolutionary and Nationalist elder.

梁鸿志.note: 1882–1946; head of the Japanese-sponsored 'Reformed Government' at Nanjing (1938); executed as a traitor after the war.

方君瑛.note: Elder sister of Fang Junbi and a fellow Tongmenghui revolutionary; took part in the 1910 plot against the Qing Prince Regent.

黎仲实.note: Tongmenghui revolutionary, a co-conspirator in the 1910 attempt on the Qing Prince Regent.

俞云纪.note: A revolutionary who joined the 1910 plot against the Prince Regent and fell at the Canton (Huanghuagang) rising of 1911.

丹娜.note: The French–Annamese ('métisse') woman who drove Chen to Haiphong as cover on his escape from Hanoi; romanization uncertain.

袁伯勋.note: One of the three Hanoi action-team men captured (a cover-passport name).

孙亚东.note: One of the three Hanoi action-team men captured (a cover-passport name).

杨卫河.note: One of the three Hanoi action-team men captured (a cover-passport name).

王兆槐.note: Chen's old friend; commander of the Juntong's directly-subordinate Special Service Regiment at Chongqing, at whose Wanglongmen home Chen lodged on his recall.

王持平.note: Wang Zhaohuai's wife and Wang Yunsun's elder sister; the matchmaker of Chen's own marriage.

周伟龙.note: Chief clerk (书记长) of the Juntong headquarters, nominally senior to Mao Renfeng; had stopped coming to work by 1939.

徐钟奇.note: Chief of the Judicial sub-section under Chen's Third Section; years later a detention-house warden, when Chen in turn became his prisoner.

赵世瑞.note: Chen's schoolmate; chief of the Inspection Office of the Chongqing Garrison Headquarters, a post first meant for Chen.

陶一珊.note: Deputy chief of the Inspection Office of the Chongqing Garrison Headquarters.

赵理君.note: Acting chief of the Shanghai District and leader of its First Action Squad; on sick leave and transferred to Luoyang in 1939.

胡尚武.note: Assistant secretary of the Shanghai District.

潘其武.note: Secretary of Dai Li's residence (公馆秘书).

王飞.note: Styled Chongtian (冲天); the principal of Chen's middle school, later a fellow trainee at the Central Training Corps.

帅崇兴.note: Colonel; commander of the First Student Corps of the Fifth Term at Chen's military academy, a fellow trainee in 1939.

朱啸谷.note: Leader of the First Group of the Shanghai District intelligence section.

刘俊卿.note: Of the International Settlement police-house; a contact in the effort to rescue Wang Luqiao.

刘绍奎.note: Of the International Settlement police-house; a contact in the effort to rescue Wang Luqiao.

王亢子.note: Also called Chanhong (蝉红); elder daughter of Wang Tianmu, a fellow-sufferer of Chen's wife in the mid-1930s imprisonments.

王因子.note: Also called Chanlü (蝉绿); younger (third) daughter of Wang Tianmu, acquainted with Wang Luqiao, whose Shanghai tryst led to his arrest.

犬养健.note: Japanese politician of the Seiyūkai and son of former premier Inukai Tsuyoshi; Kagesa's aide in escorting Wang Jingwei from Hanoi.

犬养毅.note: Prime minister of Japan assassinated by naval officers in 1932; father of Inukai Ken.

周隆庠.note: Wang Jingwei's interpreter, who carried word between Wang and Kagesa at Hanoi.

有田八郎.note: Japanese foreign minister at the time of Wang Jingwei's June 1939 Tokyo visit.

西尾寿造.note: Japanese general; inspector-general of education, made commander-in-chief of the China Expeditionary Army in September 1939.

佐藤贤了.note: Japanese officer; deputy chief of staff of the South China Expeditionary Army, who helped Wang Jingwei's Shanghai activity.

陈调元.note: Former chairman of the Anhui provincial government; his house at No. 76 Jessfield Road became a Wang-regime venue.

邓龙光.note: Cantonese Nationalist general, courted by Wang Jingwei for a South China regime but unmoved.

矢野征记.note: Secretary of the Japanese Foreign Ministry (the 矢野 of the Kagesa memoir), part of the Wang defection party.

清水董三.note: Secretary of the Japanese Foreign Ministry, part of the Wang Jingwei Tokyo party.

谷垣专一.note: Kagesa Sadaaki's son-in-law, who with Kuraoka edited his posthumous manuscripts.

仓冈克行.note: Kagesa Sadaaki's secretary, who with Tanigaki edited his posthumous manuscripts.

板垣征四郎.note: Japanese general (1885–1948), Kwantung Army architect of the 1931 Manchurian seizure, war minister, later chief of staff of the China Expeditionary Army; hanged as a war criminal. The source writes his surname variously 板垣 / 坂垣 / 扳垣 (see 坂垣征四郎).

陈三才.note: Wu County engineer and patriot (Tsinghua, Westinghouse); a volunteer in the Wang case, martyred at Nanjing on 2 Oct 1940.

黄逸光.note: Overseas-Chinese airman of Mexico; recruited into the Juntong to sanction Wang Jingwei, martyred at Nanjing on 17 Dec 1940.

戴静园.note: Original name Dai Xingbing (戴星炳); a major-general adviser to the Military Affairs Commission who volunteered with Wu Gengshu, executed at Yuhuatai on 21 Mar 1940.

邵明贤.note: Hangzhou-trained police officer; martyred at Nanjing on 17 Dec 1940 in the Wang case.

陈群.note: Puppet politician; 'Chairman of Jiangsu Province' under the Wang regime, whose Yuyuan Road houses Wang used.

邓演达.note: Leader of the 'Third Party' (Provisional Action Committee of the Kuomintang); arrested in Shanghai 1931 and executed by the Nationalists.

钱新民.note: Chief of the Juntong's Nanjing District, the other unit charged with sanctioning Wang Jingwei.

王钟岳.note: Cover name 'Wang Le' (王乐); chief of the Hanoi wireless station, the link to Chongqing.

陈石生.note: A contact-man who presented Dai Jingyuan to Wang Jingwei; possibly of Wang's wife's kindred.

陈耀祖.note: Wang Jingwei's brother-in-law; wrote to Huang Yiguang urging him to join the 'Peace Movement.'

唐骏圻.note: A Kaohsiung correspondent (styled Mr. Tang) whose letters supplied Chen with information on Chen Bangguo and Chen Buyun and corrected the Chen/Zheng Bangguo name.

王伯群.note: Former Minister of Communications; owner of the Lane 1136 Yuyuan Road houses Wang Jingwei used.

吴四宾.note: Source writes 吴四宾 (digitization glitch for 吴四宝); a No. 76 figure who, with Li Shiqun, moved into Wang's former Yuyuan Road house.

周至柔.note: Nationalist air-force general; dean of studies at the Air Force Officers' School.

王叔铭.note: Nationalist air-force general; chief of the education section at the Air Force Officers' School.

刘守法.note: Airman and memoirist whose essay on Huang Yiguang Chen quotes.

刘方雄.note: A Hong Kong chief of the Juntong during the war; author of a book on the intelligence 'peace talks.'

韩继文.note: Styled Shangying (尚英); Chen's Military Academy classmate who once saved his life and reported Cen Jiazhuo's death.

陈第容.note: Assistant secretary in charge of personnel at the Shanghai District when Chen took over in 1939; his betrayal of the organization's secrets set off the enemy search of fourteen District offices. Romanization mine.

黄志远.note: An old comrade-in-arms of Chen's who kept the occupation-era pages of the Xin Shen Bao and Zhonghua Ribao reproducing the enemy's exposé of the Shanghai District, and contributed them to this book. Romanization mine.

万里浪.note: Deputy leader (or leader) of the Shanghai District's Fourth Action Brigade; turned traitor in October 1939 and became First Section chief of the puppet 'No. 76.' Romanization mine.

刘时雍.note: Leader of the Shanghai District's Fourth Action Brigade, at odds with his deputy Wan Lilang. Romanization mine.

蒋安华.note: Leader of the Shanghai District's Third Action Brigade, a Military Academy classmate of Chen's from Guizhou; the District's mainstay brigade. Romanization mine.

吉震苍.note: Leader of the Shanghai District's Second Action Brigade (cover name Zhao Sheng), the brigade tied to Du Yuesheng. Romanization mine.

毕高奎.note: Leader of the Shanghai District's 'New Group One,' a France-trained mechanical and electrical engineer; also written Bi Haokui (毕镐奎). Romanization mine.

孙大成.note: Cover name of the leader of the Shanghai 'Anti-Japanese Traitor-Killing Corps'; lost an arm to an explosive at the Bund Park and became a one-armed hero. Still in service when Chen wrote (1983), so his true name is withheld. Romanization mine.

刘健.note: Leader of the Shanghai District's Second Intelligence Group, a senior comrade from Hunan. Romanization mine.

萧杰英.note: Woman courier and head of the Shanghai District's inner courier station; sister of Xiao Zhangquan, of the martyr Xiao family. Romanization mine.

萧张权.note: Youngest of the eight Shanghai District action-brigade leaders (Eighth Brigade); died under torture by the Japanese gendarmerie at Suzhou. Romanization mine.

张璜.note: Accountant of the Shanghai District headquarters, with Zheng Xiuyuan during the July 1939 dance-hall escape. Romanization mine.

杨震裔.note: Chief Wireless Inspector of the Shanghai District; later held posts in the Intelligence Bureau and the Bureau of Investigation in Taiwan. Romanization mine.

陈明楚.note: Cover name of Chen Dirong (陈第容), the assistant secretary whose defection exposed the Shanghai District. Romanization mine.

戴藏宜.note: Son of Dai Li; the Dai and Wang families were once spoken of as prospective in-laws.

翁光辉.note: First chief of the Shanghai District, in the early-1930s Special Services Department era. Romanization mine.

吴乃宪.note: Second chief of the Shanghai District, styled Jinfu, of the first class of the Whampoa Military Academy; later a National Assembly delegate. Figures in 'Rooting Out Traitors in the North.'

王世英.note: An intelligence compiler-reviewer of the Shanghai District, promoted from code clerk. Romanization mine.

潘绍岳.note: Leader of the Shanghai District's Sixth Action Brigade, an outstanding figure. Romanization mine.

杜月笙.note: The pre-eminent boss of the Shanghai Green Gang (1888-1951); his 'students' staffed the Shanghai District's Second Action Brigade. Glossed in the note at the Du residence (ch17).

程海涛.note: Chinese chief inspector of the political department of the French Concession police; sanctioned by the Shanghai District on 18 October 1939 for leading searches of its offices. Romanization mine.

耿嘉基.note: Courtesy name Jizhi; a French Concession official ('Secretary Geng') the Shanghai District was ordered to sanction; a 'second-rate notable' who shot himself in 1943. Romanization mine.

王一新.note: Shanghai District secretary briefly after Zheng Xiuyuan; a Russia-trained ex-Communist, transferred out at Chen’s request. Romanization mine.

马河图.note: Leader of Wang Tianmu’s three Tianjin bodyguards; carried out the Christmas 1939 sanction of Chen Dirong and He Xingjian, then returned to the rear. Romanization mine.

岳清江.note: One of Wang Tianmu’s three bodyguards. Romanization mine.

丁寳龄.note: The youngest of Wang Tianmu’s three bodyguards. Romanization mine.

何行健.note: Also named He Tianfeng; a Loyal and Patriotic Army commander turned puppet “lieutenant-general,” shot dead beside Chen Dirong at the Weldon Dance Hall, Christmas 1939. Romanization mine.

何天风.note: Another name of He Xingjian (何行健). Romanization mine.

汪秋芳.note: Cover name Wang Fang; a foreign-affairs-trained woman agent sent by Dai Li to the Shanghai District early in 1940. Romanization mine.

汪芳.note: Cover name of the woman agent Wang Qiufang (汪秋芳). Romanization mine.

田淑君.note: A woman of intelligence aptitude, 'of the household' of the former Shanghai garrison commander Yang Hu; Dai Li had her penetrate the Wang regime, then suspected a genuine defection. Romanization mine.

傅胜蓝.note: Chief of the Qingdao Station who turned traitor; the target of the woman agent Ding Wenhui’s failed poisoning. Romanization mine.

丁文蕙.note: A young woman agent of the Qingdao Station charged with poisoning the traitor Fu Shenglan; caught and strangled by him. Romanization mine.

俞叶封.note: Puppet chairman of the Shanghai General Chamber of Commerce; sanctioned by the Shanghai District on 14 January 1940 (recounted in the next chapter). Romanization mine.

虞洽卿.note: 1867–1945; a leading Shanghai comprador-businessman and community leader, honored as “the venerable Yu.” Chen cites him to refute a rumor that Dai Li had ordered his sanction.

贺耀组.note: 1889–1961; the nominal director of the Bureau of Investigation and Statistics, a figurehead while Dai Li ran its affairs as deputy director.

褚民谊.note: 1884–1946; a senior figure of the Wang Jingwei regime (deputy president of its Executive Yuan, then foreign minister); executed for treason after the war. New Group One planted an agent at his side.

万墨林.note: Du Yuesheng's cousin and business manager, a Green Gang figure; his memoir 'Bygone Days in Shanghai' (沪上往事) is quoted here on the collaborator Yu Yefeng.

傅炳宸.note: Head of the “special liaison station” relaying between the Shanghai District and Wu XX; a fifth-class Military Academy man. Romanization mine.

傅式说.note: Former president of Daxia University who joined the Wang regime; New Group One recruited two of his secretaries. The source misprints his surname 傅 as 传.

邵飘萍.note: Inner-duty head of the Shanghai District’s Second Action Team; the source notes he bore the same name as the famous journalist Shao Piaowei (killed 1926) but was a different man. Romanization mine.

张圣才.note: Leader of the Shanghai District’s Third Intelligence Group, who could identify the traitor Geng Jiaji. Romanization mine.

陈默.note: An action man of the Shanghai District’s Second Brigade; took part in sanctioning Yu Yefeng and Qian Renlong. Romanization mine.

赵刚义.note: Leader of the Third Action Team of the puppet No. 76, sanctioned 8 December 1939. Romanization mine.

钱人龙.note: Deputy chief of the confidential office of the puppet No. 76, sanctioned 26 February 1940. Romanization mine.

伊凡诺夫.note: The White Russian who betrayed the martyr Chen Sancai to the enemy; sanctioned by New Group One on 18 September 1941.

顾兰君.note: A 1930s Shanghai film actress; Chen rented her former apartment on Seymour Road.

杨虎.note: 1889–1966; former Songhu (Shanghai) garrison commander, notorious for his part in the 1927 anti-Communist purge; Tian Shujun was “of his household.”

范纪曼.note: Another name of Fan Xing (范行), the mysterious intelligence source. Romanization mine.

劳勃生.note: The source gives only the Chinese transliteration 劳勃生 of a Western (probably British) surname—likely something like Robertson or Robinson—of the Shanghai Municipal Police political section; the original form is not certain, so the romanization is of the Chinese as given.

袁殊.note: Also called Xueyi (学易) and Xiaoyi (筱易); a journalist-agent of tangled loyalties, later revealed as a Communist.

新艳秋.note: A celebrated Peking-opera actress of the female (dan) roles, performing at the Gengxin Stage on the night of Yu Yefeng's sanction.

吴世宝.note: Alias Yunfu (云甫); an underworld figure and first commander of No. 76's guard corps, later poisoned.

胡均鹤.note: Chief of the Second Section of No. 76, later found to be a Communist as well.

傅也文.note: Secretary-general of No. 76, installed at the recommendation of Li Shiqun's wife; later found to be a Communist. Romanization mine.

蒋福田.note: A working connection of the Shanghai District within the French Concession police. Romanization mine.

秦启荣.note: A Shandong man of the sixth Whampoa class, named in Dai Li's directive to command the Tianjin-Pukou demolition brigade and organize the Qingdao action group.

潘汉年.note: The Chinese Communist Party's foremost intelligence operative in occupied Shanghai, who worked the seam between the underground and the Wang puppets' No. 76.

聂崇侯.note: A Jiangxi-born, German-trained doctor of ophthalmology in Shanghai whom Chen recruited to interpret with the German arms-keeper. Romanization mine.

潘子欣.note: "Master Pan the Seventh," a Jiangsu-born Tianjin notable (keeper of the National Grand Hotel) living hidden in Shanghai; called "the Du Yuesheng of Tianjin." Romanization mine.

兪叶封.note: Variant-glyph spelling (兪 for 俞) of Yu Yefeng, the collaborator sanctioned at the Gengxin Stage in January 1940 (ch24).

丁默邨.note: Co-founder and director of the puppet Special Operations Headquarters (No. 76) with Li Shiqun; tried and executed as a traitor after the war.

汪时璟.note: North China's foremost economic collaborator; the Kang Corps' unfinished target (see Part One, ch06). Rendered Wang Shiying consistently across the book.

施何成.note: A New Group One operative (aliases Bao Yueren, later Peng Jun); his letters supply several of the chapter's martyr cases.

邵范九.note: A cousin's nephew of the KMT elder Shao Lizi; sanctioned in November 1939 for going over to the puppets.

陶联芳.note: A New Group One member, buried alive by the puppet Huzhou Station after being caught re-linking with the Bureau.

徐寿新.note: Alias Zhu Chengwo; chief communications inspector of the Shanghai District, shot at No. 76 on 25 Dec 1939. The reproduced Xu Wenqi essay memorializes him.

朱承我.note: Alias of the martyr Xu Shouxin, taken to keep the memory of his late wife Zhu Cheng'e.

徐寿棪.note: Xu Shouxin's younger brother, a Juntong veteran; his letters recovered his brother's martyrdom for this book.

徐文祺.note: A Shanghai District assistant secretary imprisoned with Xu Shouxin at No. 76; author of the reproduced memorial essay.

余延智.note: Fifth Action Brigade commander (surname perhaps Chu), killed with Xu Shouxin at No. 76 in December 1939.

周锡良.note: A counter-espionage operative inside No. 76, killed there in December 1939; the puppet verdict writes his name with a different middle character (周希良), alike in sound.

张执一.note: A CCP united-front operative under the Jiangsu Provincial Committee, later deputy head of the Party's Central United Front Work Department; author of the quoted memoir 'In the Heart of the Enemy.'

赤木亲之.note: Japanese deputy commissioner of the Shanghai Municipal Police, assassinated on Yuyuan Road, June 1941.

林秀澄.note: Lieutenant-colonel, chief of the Special Higher Section of the Shanghai Japanese Gendarmerie; the 'Section chief Lin' Chen knew only by surname.

李正梁.note: Alias Li Liang; leader of the Third Action Brigade's Fourth Group, who directed the Akagi assassination.

李亮.note: The everyday name of Li Zhengliang, director of the Akagi case.

林怀部.note: The hired bodyguard who shot the tycoon Zhang Xiaolin dead in October 1940; the mysteries around him open ch27.

俞作柏.note: Deputy commander-in-chief of the Loyal and Patriotic Army, addressed in one of Dai Li's quoted telegrams.

林之江.note: A No. 76 executioner (with Wan Lilang) of Xu Shouxin; later turned back to the government and died in poverty at Hong Kong.

萧焕文.note: The Hunan-born patriarch of the Xiao family, whose whole household served the Juntong; kept the Loyal Army's liaison.

陈植琚.note: Xiao Shuying's husband; leader of the Dachang field group, blown to death by an enemy plane early in the war.

李鑫.note: A Shanghai Kang Corps action man who perished with his own bomb at the Jessfield Park Axis-recognition rally, August 1941.

缪维.note: A Kang Corps operative killed with Huang Kezhong when their charge went off at Hongkou Park.

黄克忠.note: A Kang Corps action man (also recorded as Huang Ruitang); took part in the Tōwa Theater bombing and died at Hongkou Park.

向松坡.note: A prominent Hong Gang chief in Shanghai (styled Haiqian) whose connection the CCP operative Zhang Zhiyi used.

赵圣.note: The working name of the Second Action Brigade's commander (real name Ji Zhencang, keyed); the man who reported the Zhang Xiaolin sanction. Rendered Zhao Sheng consistently.

黄金荣.note: The third of the Green Gang's 'Three Tycoons' of Shanghai, beside Du Yuesheng and Zhang Xiaolin (see ch04).

朱升.note: The servant who killed the puppet Shanghai mayor Fu Xiao'an with an axe on 11 Oct 1940; central to ch28 Section 2. His assassination act was noted at ch04. Source spelling-variants (朱生, 朱升源) and the alias 陈中南 render inline.

周西垣.note: The third-sub-brigade leader of the First Action Brigade, turned by Wan Lilang; the trap through which Liu Yuanshen was taken. Cover name 冯贤 (Feng Xian), keyed separately.

冯贤.note: Cover name of Zhou Xiyuan; the source uses it as such (此人名叫冯贤(周西垣的化名)), so it renders 'Feng Xian', not 'Zhou Xiyuan'.

朱敏.note: Zhou Xiyuan's unit secretary and the informant who denounced him; the foil of Liu Yuanshen's memoir.

刘全德.note: First-sub-brigade leader, a Jiangxi man and former Ruijin 'Little Red Devil'; killed in Shanghai after the government moved to Taiwan.

相强伟.note: Second-sub-brigade leader, a man of Sheng County in Zhejiang.

骆成金.note: Xiang Qiangwei's deputy, out of the Hangzhou Police Academy; tortured on the tiger bench at No. 76 without confessing.

许力求.note: Director of the South China Evening News, Wang Jingwei's Hong Kong propaganda organ; the sanction target Zhou Xiyuan dangles as bait.

褚亚鹏.note: Formerly a courier of the Beiping station, transferred to Shanghai; he ran an electrical shop on Bubbling Well Road as a Shanghai District liaison station. Arrested a month before Chen and brought to No. 76 to identify him, he did not point Chen out.

林焕芝.note: The Cantonese-speaking chief of the action section at No. 76, formerly of the Shanghai District Fourth Team; his elder brother Lin Zhencheng was of the Third Team.

姜绍谟.note: Courtesy name Cilie; Chief of the Shanghai Reserve District (the Second District), who had lain concealed in Shanghai without his identity being exposed, and who took over the Shanghai work after Chen's capture and carried it on to the victory of the war of resistance.

叶剑英.note: The Communist representative on the Military Mediation Executive Headquarters at Beiping and chief of staff of the Communist army; later a marshal of the People's Republic.

刘培初.note: Corps Commander of the Ministry of National Defense Pacification Corps and head of its Student Corps; author of the posthumous memoir Fleeting Glimpses of a Floating Life, quoted here. Earlier he had led the Wuhan practice corps in which Chen trained (see Part Three, chapter ten).

李宗仁.note: 1891-1969; a leading Guangxi general, director of the Chairman's Beiping Field Headquarters, and later, in 1949, acting President of the Republic of China.

傅作义.note: 1895-1974; commander-in-chief of the North China Bandit Suppression Headquarters and the Nationalist defender of Beiping, which he surrendered by negotiated agreement to the Communists in January 1949, sparing the city a siege.

计兆祥.note: A wireless operator of the First Brigade's stay-behind work left in Beiping; he shot himself to resist arrest, one of the few of the stay-behind party whose fate Chen could trace.

李玉林.note: Deputy commander of Chen's First Brigade, a fellow East-Hebei man and, in the War of Resistance, chief of staff of the Sixth Route Army of the North China Loyal and Patriotic Army; imprisoned and tortured by the Japanese, he survived and was called 'Fifth Brother' by his fellow prisoners. One of the three 'pillars' of the brigade.

罗敬.note: The First Brigade's political director, and the calligrapher who inscribed the covers and title-leaves of all five Nameless Heroes volumes; a Fu Jen University graduate gravely wounded by a bomb-splinter at Chongqing in 1941. A 'pillar' of the brigade.

侯腾.note: Courtesy name Feixia; one of the two deputy chiefs of the Second Bureau of the Ministry of National Defense, in Zheng Jiemin's command chain over the Pacification Corps.

吴安之.note: An old Beiping-Tianjin colleague of Chen's, now chief of the police department of the Ping-Han Railway Administration Bureau; he met Chen at Xiyuan airfield on his return.

马汉三.note: Appointed by Dai Li director of the Juntong's Beiping Office after the victory, then Chief of the Bureau of Civil Affairs of the Beiping Municipal Government; his residence was the very Meizha Hutong house of the 1938 Wang Kemin operation.

张家铨.note: Leader of the 'Cangzhou Section' in the early 1930s, now a major-general and chief of the Second Section of the Beiping Field Headquarters.

史泓.note: An old directly subordinate courier of the Beiping Station, now a major-general and chief of the Second Section of the North China Bandit Suppression Headquarters.

陈诚.note: 1898-1965; one of Chiang Kai-shek's most trusted generals and, at this time, Chief of the General Staff (Chen corrects here his fourth volume's misattribution of the post to Bai Chongxi, who was Minister of National Defense).

聂恩俊.note: The First Brigade's quartermaster major, a Hefei man and graduate of the Quartermaster School, drawn from the Sixth Depot Superintendency; Chen flags him to revisit.

李鸣秋.note: Chen's Whampoa schoolmate, an early Communist imprisoned nine years, used in 1948 as the go-between to reach Lin Biao and Tao Zhu; the pivot of the chapter.

李运昌.note: A Zunhua man and East-Hebei guerrilla chief in the war years, later a CCP general and Minister of Railways.

罗荣桓.note: Political commissar of the Communist Northeast field army, senior in the Party to Lin Biao; later a PLA marshal. Zheng Jiemin warns Chen to avoid his intervention.

黄郛.note: The diplomat (courtesy Yingbai) who acted for He Yingqin at Beiping in the early 1930s as chairman of the Executive Yuan's Beiping Political Affairs Reorganization Committee.

安春山.note: Commander of the Provisional Third Army and a favored general of Fu Zuoyi's; led in person the cavalry-spearheaded raid on Anguo that narrowly missed Mao Zedong.

朱占奎.note: Magistrate of Anci County (concurrently a Hebei district commissioner); an ex-Communist military-sub-district commander captured and turned, who defected back to the Communists in 1948.

刘玉珠.note: A fixer and friend of the deputy brigade commander who made the brigade a 'gift' of some 2,000 Japanese rifles, and was later detained and tried in the same corruption case as Ma Hansan.

萧润宇.note: A member of the First Directly Subordinate Section; author of the 'Record of the Work' quoted at length in section three.

牛广金.note: A member of the Shijiazhuang work-group, wounded by a shell-fragment and captured; author of the 'Brief Record of the Shijiazhuang Work' quoted in section four.

吕正操.note: Communist commander of the Central Hebei Military District, which held the Beiping-Tianjin-Baoding triangle from 1938; later a PLA general.

常绍曾.note: Leader of the North-Suburb Mixed Group and afterward the West-Suburb Group; a graduate of the Japanese Military Academy and once Chen's own pupil; author of three accounts quoted in section two.

田英杰.note: Squad leader of the North-Suburb intelligence squad, the 'Captain Tian' of the Battle of Lishuiqiao; author of the quoted first-person account of that night's fight and break-out.

卢德明.note: A directly-subordinate member attached to the Beiping Field Headquarters' unit at Shimen; author of the quoted account of the Communist assault on and capture of Shimen.

刘子元.note: Commander of the Daxing county self-defense brigade at Lishuiqiao; a former follower of the North China Loyal and Patriotic Army.

冯玉柱.note: Chang Shaozeng's successor as leader of the North-Suburb Group; on the battle night he went into Beiping to lay the urgent report and summon the cavalry relief.

王抚洲.note: Also called Wang Zhenwu; a Young China Party man who ran the Third Route Army of the Loyal and Patriotic Army in Shandong, a National Assembly delegate, later a vice-minister of economic affairs in Taiwan.

白家祺.note: A lieutenant colonel, brigade-attached; author of the piece 'The Battle of Moxingling' in the Hong Kong magazine Guohun, whose verse opens the Lishuiqiao section.

杜心吾.note: The renowned martial artist of Cili in Hunan (his name properly written 杜心五); 'dragon head' of the Hongmen's Qixia Mountain lodge and a senior of the Green Gang, under whom Chen and Cheng Yanqiu were briefly enrolled as disciples.

程艳秋.note: The great Peking-opera dan (his stage name also written 程砚秋), one of the 'Four Great Dan'; here Chen's fellow 'disciple' under Du Xinwu, who in 1947-48 pressed Chen to intercede for detainees.

汪鸿翥.note: First commander of the First Brigade's directly subordinate assault team; author of the account quoted in section two of the team's forming and its battles about Beiping and Tianjin.

吴春祥.note: Third commander of the directly subordinate assault team; author of the section-four account of the march and withdrawal between Yangliuqing, Wangqingtuo, and Tang'erli on the night Zhu Zhankui defected.

谷守林.note: Staff officer of the Second Command Room, who called with Chang Shaozeng upon Zhu Zhankui; sent by Chen to Hong Kong on mainland work in 1951, he lost his reason and vanished without trace.

萧克.note: He Long's deputy as commander of the 120th Division of the Eighth Route Army; the senior Communist commander in the Hebei-Rehe border region to whose forces Zhu Zhankui was sent after 1945.

王兆芬.note: Commanding officer of the First Command Room, seated at Zhuoxian; author of the long account quoted in section one of the opening-up of the work and the aftermath of the Laishui campaign. (The source glitches the surname 主兆芬 once; one man.)

张鲁颖.note: Commanding officer of the Fifth Command Room at Zhangyuan and later brigade-adjutant for liaison to the North China Bandit-Suppression Headquarters; author of the section-2 account of the Chahar-Suiyuan work.

陈振山.note: Commander of the Second Brigade in the Northeast; Chen's companion on the journey to the Nanjing conference, with whom he made the compact for a Northeast fallback. Lost in the Northeast fighting, his fate never confirmed.

孟广第.note: Leader of the Baoding Group under the First Command Room; author of the short account of the Zhuoxian 'Cleanliness and Hygiene' / 'Cleanse-the-Source, Root-Out-Traitors' movement.

鲁英庆.note: Commander of the 35th Army who, following his division commander Li Mingding, took his own life at the Zhangfeidian station in the Laishui campaign. The source misprints the given name as 鲁英尘 and 鲁英屡 elsewhere; one man.

郭景云.note: Successor commander of the 35th Army, who took his own life at the fall of Xinbao'an on 24 December 1948 — the army's second commander to die by his own hand for his country.

孙兰峰.note: Commander of the 11th Army Group garrisoning Zhangyuan; after the destruction of the 35th Army he broke out in two columns, of whose fifty thousand and more only a few thousand reached Guisui.

李铭鼎.note: Division commander under Lu Yingqing in the 35th Army; hampered by the guarding of prisoners, his division met defeat at Laishui, and he took his own life first.

李中庸.note: Administrative inspector-commissioner (probably of the Second district), a former Chongqing colleague of Wang Zhaofen's, who drew the First Command Room into training the district's administrative cadres.

王凤岗.note: The hard-driving anti-Communist commissioner whose district was praised as the 'iron triangle of Beiping-Tianjin-Baoding'; he sought out Wang Zhaofen for the pacification work and died later in a Taiwan prison.

王智斌.note: Leader of the 'Tianjin Intelligence Group'; a Northeast-born, Japanese-educated former puppet interpreter who, of the three men who set out together, 'took the crooked road,' was taken by the Communists off the Shandong coast, went over to them, and vanished after Yang Fan's purge. Also named 王紫斌 Wang Zibin.

齐枕萍.note: Member of the 'Tianjin Intelligence Group'; recommended by Chen to the 'Central Second Section' under Zheng Jiemin, where he worked thirty years, dying of illness in 1986. (Written 齐枕平 in the earlier chapters; one man.)

郭子中.note: Member of the 'Tianjin Intelligence Group'; a Harbin-raised man of a simpler, honester sort who fled to Japan and, unable to remain when his papers ran out, was deported to the mainland.

洪复予.note: The draftsman of the First Pacification Brigade (earlier of the Shanghai Station), who made the home-made enemy-order charts that hung in the brigade-headquarters office; after his discharge he worked decades in an advertising firm and died alone, unmarried, in Taiwan.

军统.note: Short for the Bureau of Investigation and Statistics of the Military Affairs Commission (军事委员会调查统计局), the Nationalist military secret service under Dai Li; rendered 'the Juntong' throughout. See the note at the third introduction.

力行社.note: The 'Society for Vigorous Practice of the Three Principles of the People' (三民主义力行社), a secret Whampoa-clique organization of 1932, popularly the 'Blue Shirts.'

特务处.note: The covert-operations department of the Lixingshe, headed by Dai Li; the operational seed of the Juntong.

调查统计局.en: the Bureau of Investigation and Statistics
调查统计局.note: The Military Affairs Commission bureau (1932) whose Second Department, under Dai Li, grew into the Juntong.

抗日杀奸团.note: A patriotic assassination group of young people in occupied North China.

特工总部.note: The Wang regime's secret police, known from its address as 'No. 76.'

复兴社.note: A wider outer body of the Lixingshe (the 'Blue Shirts'); reorganized in 1938, together with the Lixingshe, into the Three People's Principles Youth Corps.

中统.note: The Kuomintang party's civilian secret service (Central Statistics Bureau), grown from the Party Central's Investigation Section and run by the Chen brothers' 'CC Clique'; the rival of Dai Li's military Juntong. See the note in Section 1.

关东军.note: The Japanese army stationed in the Northeast, driver of the 1931 Manchurian seizure and the 1933 invasion of Rehe; largely autonomous of Tokyo.

满洲国.note: The Japanese puppet state set up in the Northeast in 1932 under the last Qing emperor, Puyi. See the note at 'a second Manchukuo.'

北平军分会.note: The Beiping Branch of the National Military Affairs Commission (军事委员会北平分会), the top Nationalist military organ in North China, headed at this time by acting deputy chairman He Yingqin.

中国人民反法西斯大同盟.en: the Chinese People's Anti-Fascist Grand Alliance
中国人民反法西斯大同盟.note: The anti-Japanese, Communist-linked front Ji Hongchang helped organize at Tianjin in 1934.

察哈尔民众抗日同盟军.en: the Chahar People's Anti-Japanese Allied Army
察哈尔民众抗日同盟军.note: The anti-Japanese coalition Feng Yuxiang raised in Chahar in 1933, which Chen treats as Communist-penetrated; renamed, after Feng's withdrawal, the 'Anti-Japanese, Chiang-Chastising Army.'

蓝衣社.note: Outsiders' name for the Lixingshe / Renaissance Society; glossed at its first appearance.

南昌行营调查课.en: the Investigation Section of the Nanchang Field Headquarters

华北政务委员会.en: the North China Political Affairs Council

冀北边区保安司令.en: Peace-Preservation Commander of the Northern Hebei Border Region

滦榆游击总部.note: The Juntong guerrilla command for the Luan River and Shanhaiguan (Yuguan) region of East Hebei.

满铁株式会社.note: The Japanese 'Mantetsu,' a vast semi-official enterprise and instrument of Japanese expansion in China.

国民参政会.note: A wartime advisory body of the National Government.

国防部情报局.en: the Intelligence Bureau of the Ministry of National Defense
国防部情报局.note: The postwar successor organization to the Juntong.

太古公司.note: The British 'Taikoo' trading and shipping firm.

五相会议.note: Inner council of the Japanese cabinet (premier, war, navy, foreign, finance ministers), set up 1938.

兴亚院.note: The Asia Development Board, central organ for Japanese policy in occupied China, established December 1938.

临澧训练班.note: A Juntong training class at Linli, Hunan, headed by Dai Li with Yu Lexing as deputy.

同盟会.note: The Revolutionary Alliance founded by Sun Yat-sen at Tokyo in 1905, forerunner of the Nationalist Party.

民报.note: The Tongmenghui's organ ('People's Journal'), on which Wang wrote as 'Jingwei.'

光复会.note: A rival revolutionary body (Guangfuhui) set up by Zhang Taiyan and Tao Chengzhang.

保皇党.note: The Emperor-Protection party of Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao, opposed to the revolutionaries.

国际问题研究所.note: An intelligence body under Wang Fansheng specializing in international intelligence.

东方汇理银行.note: The Bank of Indochina, the French colonial bank of issue in Hanoi.

南华日报.note: The Hong Kong Chinese daily run by the Wang Jingwei faction, which floated the 'Blue Shirt Society' theory of the Hanoi killing.

西南运输公司.note: A Nationalist wartime transport organ, with a Hong Kong branch, with which Dai Li had ties.

特务团.note: A combat unit directly under the Juntong, commanded by Wang Zhaohuai at Chongqing.

中央训练团.note: The Nationalist party-and-government training organ at Chongqing; Chen attended the Third Term of its Party-Government Training Class.

政友会.note: The Friends of Constitutional Government Party, a major pre-war Japanese political party.

临时政府.note: The Japanese-sponsored 'Provisional Government of the Republic of China' at Beiping (North China), headed by Wang Kemin.

维新政府.note: The Japanese-sponsored 'Reformed Government of the Republic of China' at Nanjing (Central China), headed by Liang Hongzhi.

新一组.note: A mixed intelligence-and-action unit under the Shanghai District, the liaison for Chen Sancai.

传记文学.note: Zhuanji Wenxue, the Taipei monthly in which Nameless Heroes was serialized.

忠义救国军.note: A Dai Li-led guerrilla and irregular force in the Shanghai-Jiangsu-Zhejiang region during the war; the Shanghai District liaised with its Shanghai office.

上海职工运动委员会.note: The labor-movement organ Dai Li ordered set up in 1940, with the notables Yu Qiaqing and Zhao Zigang as figurehead members; it never really took shape.

抗团.note: The standard abbreviation of the Anti-Japanese Traitor-Killing Corps (抗日杀奸团, NOTED ch02/ch11).

联合准备银行.note: The North China puppet regime's central bank of issue (Federal Reserve Bank of China, 1938); Wang Shiying its governor. Distinct from the Wang regime's Central Reserve Bank (中央储备银行).

会审公廨.note: The Shanghai concessions' pre-1930 joint tribunal, abolished by the two reproduced retrocession agreements and replaced by the Chinese Special District Courts.

绥靖总队.note: In full the Ministry of National Defense Pacification Corps, the postwar special force raised for the 1946-49 campaign against the Communists; Chen commanded its First Brigade in the Beiping-Tianjin region.

军事调处执行部.note: The tripartite body (American, Nationalist, and Communist) set up at Beiping in 1946 to enforce the cease-fire brokered by the Marshall Mission.

军事三人小组.note: The three-man committee of Marshall, Zhang Qun for the government, and Zhou Enlai for the Communists, that directed the 1946 truce negotiations.

励志训练班.note: The training class at the Central Training Corps in Nanjing through which the cadres of the Pacification Corps were passed; see the note on the Lizhi Plan.

保密局.note: In full the Bureau of Secrets (保密局) of the Ministry of National Defense, the postwar successor to the Juntong (Bureau of Investigation and Statistics) after its 1946 reorganization; headed by Mao Renfeng. Chen served it as leader of the Beiping directly subordinate section while commanding the Pacification Corps' First Brigade under the separate Second Bureau.

人民服务总队.note: A Ministry of National Defense corps commanded by Liu Peichu in eastern Henan before he was moved to head the Pacification Corps; several of its cadres passed into the Lizhi Class.

交警总队.note: The Transport Police Corps (交通警察总队), the postwar rebadging of the Loyal and Patriotic Army as 'transport police'; in Chen's account it was in fact given over to the suppression of the Communist rising.

华北剿匪总司令部.note: The North China Bandit-Suppression Headquarters, the Nationalist theater command that conferred the First Brigade's code-name 'Unit 0760'; built on the keyed 剿匪 'bandit-suppression'.

东北人民解放军.note: The Chinese Communist field army in the Northeast, commanded by Lin Biao with Tao Zhu as political-department director; the target of the chapter's intelligence operation.

北平.note: The name of Beijing from 1928 to 1949, after the capital moved to Nanjing.

察哈尔.note: A former province north-west of Beiping, abolished in 1952.

东交民巷.note: The walled diplomatic quarter of Beiping, extraterritorial under the 1901 Boxer Protocol. Noted at first appearance in the introductions.

六国饭店.note: 六国饭店, the 'Six Nations Hotel' in the Legation Quarter; the site of the Zhang Jingyao killing. Noted at first appearance in Section 1.

热河.note: Rehe (Jehol), the borderland province north-east of Beiping, invaded by the Kwantung Army in 1933. See the note at first appearance.

韩家潭.note: A lane in Beiping's Eight Great Hutongs pleasure quarter.

国民大饭店.note: The Tianjin French-concession hotel where the shooting took place on 9 November 1934. Chen also writes it simply 国民饭店.

利顺德饭店.note: The Astor House Hotel in the British concession; glossed at first appearance.

特别第一区.note: The former German concession at Tianjin, taken back after the First World War.

劝业场.note: A famous multi-story commercial arcade in the Tianjin French concession.

安南.note: An old name for Vietnam; here French Tonkin, in Indochina.

跑马地.note: A district of Hong Kong Island; its Chinese name means 'the racecourse ground.'

半山.note: The hillside residential quarter of Hong Kong Island.

塘沽.note: The port at the mouth of the Hai River, the sea-gate of Tianjin.

吴淞口.note: The mouth of the Huangpu, the sea approach to Shanghai.

冀东.note: The eastern part of Hebei, seat of the Japanese-sponsored puppet 'East Hebei' government.

虹口.note: A district of Shanghai north of the Suzhou Creek.

河北大经路.note: A street in the Hebei district of Tianjin.

台儿庄.note: Town in southern Shandong, site of the Chinese victory of spring 1938.

张鼓峰.note: The Zhanggufeng / Lake Khasan border clash with the USSR, July–August 1938.

珊瑚坝.note: The airfield on a sandbar in the river at Chongqing, from which Wang flew out.

上清寺.note: A district of Chongqing where Wang lodged.

美专校街.note: A street in Chongqing where Wang's Chongqing residence stood.

桂林.note: City in Guangxi where Chiang stayed in December 1938.

滇越路.note: The French-built Yunnan–Vietnam (Kunming–Haiphong) railway, the route from Yunnan into Indochina.

息烽.note: A county in Guizhou; site of the Juntong's own detention camp for its own personnel.

高朗街.note: Transliterated street in Hanoi (historically Rue Colombert); Wang Jingwei's residence was No. 27.

北极阁.note: A height at Nanjing; Wang climbed it on the Double-Ninth for his last ci.

名古屋.note: Japanese city where Wang Jingwei died of illness in 1944.

红河大桥.note: The long road-and-rail bridge over the Red (Hong) River at Hanoi, the Pont Doumer (now Long Bien); scene of the failed car chase.

打叻.note: A hill resort a few hours north of Hanoi to which Wang set out on 20 March 1939. The Biography of Dai Yunong calls it 丹道镇 'Dan Dao' and the Wang-regime memoir 三桃山 'San Tao Shan'; the three names are not reconciled in the sources.

望龙门.note: A district of Chongqing where the Special Service Regiment headquarters and Wang Zhaohuai's residence stood.

浮屠关.note: A hill district of Chongqing, site of the Central Training Corps and of a large natural air-raid shelter.

愚园路.note: A road in the Shanghai French Concession where Wang Jingwei first hid on reaching the city.

杜美路.note: A street in the Shanghai French Concession (Route/Rue Doumer, today Donghu Road); Chen lodged there opposite Du Yuesheng's residence.

极司菲尔路.note: A road on the western edge of the Shanghai settlements; No. 76 became the notorious headquarters of the Wang puppet secret service.

卡尔登公寓.note: A Shanghai apartment building, home of Chen's friend Hu Yongquan.

黄埔江.note: The river running through Shanghai (source 黄埔 for the standard 黄浦).

麦阳路.note: A Shanghai street; No. 71 was a Shanghai District office.

基隆.note: The port at the northern tip of Taiwan, a way-station on Wang Jingwei's sea passage to Shanghai.

雨花台.note: The Terrace of Raining Flowers, a hill south of Nanjing long used as an execution ground.

更新舞台.note: A Peking-opera theater on Newchwang Road in the International Settlement; the site of the Yu Yefeng sanction of January 1940.

石家庄.note: The Hebei rail-junction city, scene of the Communist siege and capture of November 1947; Chen more often calls it by its older name, Shimen.

石门.note: The older name of Shijiazhuang, used throughout this chapter.

安次.note: The Hebei county garrisoned by the First Directly Subordinate Section (its seat, Langfang lies on the Bei-Ning line).

安国.note: The Hebei county whose Temple of the Medicine King was the object of the raid meant to seize Mao Zedong.

正定.note: The town reckoned the screen of Shimen, and the northern terminus of the Zheng-Tai railway.

立水桥.note: The Daxing-county village, some thirty li north of Beiping's Andingmen, named for its cement bridge; scene of the October 1948 night battle between the local corps and the Communist militia.

大兴.note: The Hebei county north of Beiping into which the North-Suburb Group extended its pacification work; Lishuiqiao lay within it.

赵家坟.note: The base village of the North-Suburb Mixed Group, at the northeastern corner of Beiping.

王庆沱.note: The town some fifteen li west of Yangliuqing garrisoned by Zhu Zhankui's security corps; it fell to the bandit army on the night the assault team and the Second Command Room withdrew from it.

杨柳青.note: The town on the northern reach of the Jin-Pu railway near Tianjin to which the Second Command Room fell back as the working district shifted ever northward.

独流.note: The Jin-Pu-line station where the assault team detrained and awaited orders; the Second Command Room's Second Group was seated there.

静海.note: The Hebei county on the northern reach of the Jin-Pu railway where the Second Command Room was seated.

顺义.note: The county north of Beiping where the assault team, in the autumn of 1948, seized a puppet county commissar and broke up an arms-repair shop at Niulanshan.

唐官屯.note: The town in Jinghai county on the Jin-Pu line where the assault-team command was handed from Wang Hongzhu to Chang Shaozeng, and where the Second Command Room's Third Group was stationed.

涿县.note: The county southwest of Beiping on the Ping-Han line where the First Command Room had its seat; the hub of section one and the place to which Fu Zuoyi's requisitioned coffins were sent.

新保安.note: The walled town on the Ping-Sui line, southeast of Xuanhua, where Guo Jingyun's 35th Army was surrounded and destroyed between 6 and 24 December 1948.

涞水.note: The Hebei county and the campaign (the 涞水之役) in which the 35th Army bled, its commander and division commander took their lives, and the mass encoffining of the dead was carried out.

保定.note: The Hebei provincial city on the Ping-Han line; seat of the First Command Room's Baoding Group and a hub of the line's pacification work.

制裁.note: The service's euphemism for the targeted killing or execution of an enemy or traitor; kept as the book's own term.

绥靖.note: A Nationalist term for the 1946–49 civil war, casting the Communists as rebels to be pacified.

东亚新秩序.note: Japan's slogan (東亞新秩序) for a Japanese-led East Asian bloc, from Konoe's statement of 3 November 1938.

东亚协同体.note: A related Japanese slogan (東亞協同體) for the merging of Japan, 'Manchukuo,' and China.

田中奏折.note: The alleged 1927 memorial of Tanaka Giichi on world conquest; generally regarded as a forgery.

九国公约.note: The 1922 Washington treaty guaranteeing China's sovereignty and the Open Door.

马关条约.note: The 1895 treaty ending the first Sino-Japanese War.

国家总动员法.note: Japanese law of April 1938 placing the economy on a war footing.

中山舰事件.note: Chiang Kai-shek's March 1926 move against Communist influence in the Nationalist Party and army.

宁汉分裂.note: The 1927 rupture between the Nanjing (Ning) and Wuhan (Han) Nationalist governments.

五四运动.note: The 1919 nationalist and cultural movement; Chen ties it to the entry of Communism into China.

甲午战争.note: The war of 1894–95 in which Japan defeated Qing China.

琉球.note: The island kingdom annexed by Japan in 1879, cited as the start of Japan's designs on China.

北光丸.note: The Yamashita Steamship Company cargo vessel that carried Wang Jingwei from Vietnam to Shanghai in 1939.

霞飞将军.note: The French mail steamer on which Chen sailed from Hong Kong to Shanghai.

励志计划.note: The plan under which the Ministry of National Defense raised, trained, and tasked the Pacification Corps; 励志 means to steel the will or better oneself.

特种部队.note: The new-pattern special force of the Pacification Corps; the same compound is glossed 'Special Forces' in the chapter that defines it (Part Four, chapter two).

特种组织.note: The Leader's term for the older special services he had 'raised with his own hands over twenty years,' the Juntong foremost among them, whose decay he lamented at the opening of the Lizhi Class.

掏心战术.note: The code-name of the deep raid into the Communist-held triangle aimed at seizing the enemy's leadership at a stroke; the chapter title glosses it at title level.

平津保三角地带.note: The dozen-odd counties of central Hebei, bounded by Beiping, Tianjin, and Baoding, held by the Communists' Central Hebei forces from 1938.
